title: PACE: Parameter Change for Unsupervised Environment Design
claim: Prior methods judge training environments with indirect, noisy proxy signals; ours measures realized learning progress directly through parameter change.
layout: 2 panels, left problem and right method, concentric zones with arrows
description: The figure has two banner-headed panels. The left, blue "The Problem & Goal" panel shows a dashed box with a training maze above and a more complex OOD maze below. A red X marks overfitting and poor generalization between them. A robot icon asks "How to seek this Zone?" A large arrow labeled "Environment Zone" points to concentric circles: a Too Easy/Comfort Zone core, an Optimal Learning Zone ring, and a Too Hard/Panic Zone outer ring. The right, orange "Unsupervised Environment Design" panel lists prior proxy signals (regret, GAE/MC, marginal benefit) as a faded gray swirl with icons for high cost, high variance and bias. A bold blue arrow from a neural-network-and-magnifier RL agent carries the formula ||θ_new − θ_old||² and points to the zone. A checklist reads low bias, low variance, simple. A bottom banner says "Our Method (PACE): Direct Intrinsic Evaluation".
caption: Overview of Unsupervised Environment Design and the core idea of PACE. Prior UED methods rely on indirect proxy signals (e.g., regret, GAE, or Monte Carlo return) to evaluate environments, which often suffer from bias, high variance, or high computational cost. PACE directly measures agent learning progress via policy parameter change induced by environment interaction, providing a simple, low-variance, and intrinsic evaluation signal.
abstract: Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) offers a promising paradigm for improving reinforcement learning generalization by adaptively shaping training environments, but it requires reliable environment evaluation to remain effective. However, existing UED methods evaluate environments using indirect proxy signals such as regret, value-based errors, or Monte Carlo, which suffer from bias, high variance, or substantial computational overhead and fail to reflect agent realized learning progress. To address these limitations, we propose Parameter Change Environment Design (PACE), which evaluates an environment through the policy parameter change induced by training on that environment, directly grounding environment selection in realized learning progress. Specifically, PACE assigns environment value using a first-order approximation of the policy optimization objective, where the improvement induced by an environment is proportional to the squared L2 norm of the corresponding parameter update, enabling low-variance and computation-efficient evaluation without additional rollouts. Experiments on MiniGrid and Craftax show that PACE consistently outperforms established UED baselines, achieving higher IQM and smaller Optimality Gap on OOD evaluations, including an IQM of 96.4% and an Optimality Gap of 17.2% on MiniGrid.
